summary: Before Passover, knowing his hour has come, Jesus loves his own ‘to the end.’ He washes the disciples' feet, interprets the act as cleansing and a pattern of humble service, identifies the betrayer through a shared morsel, and lets Judas depart into night. Once betrayal is in motion, Jesus speaks of glory, gives the new command to love as he has loved, and predicts Peter's denial.
whyItMatters: John places the meaning of the cross in a basin and towel before narrating the arrest. Jesus's authority is not diminished by lowly service; it is expressed through it. The community's public marker is therefore neither power nor slogans but cruciform love—offered even in a room containing betrayal, confusion, and impending failure.

context.author: The anonymous Fourth Gospel narrator, opening Jesus's final meal and farewell teaching with an enacted interpretation of his death
context.audience: Readers familiar with household footwashing, purity, meal customs, and the shame attached to a servant's task
context.date: The meal occurs before Passover in John's chronology, on the eve of Jesus's death
context.setting: A private supper in Jerusalem with Jesus's closest disciples
context.literaryForm: Symbolic action, interpretive dialogue, betrayal announcement, and opening farewell instruction

outline.heading: Jesus washes the disciples' feet and answers Peter
Lord and Teacher gives a pattern of servant action
Jesus identifies the betrayer, who departs into night
Glory, the new command, and Peter's denial

keyVerses.text: If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
keyVerses.why: Jesus makes status-lowering service an obligation rooted in his own authority and example.

keyVerses.text: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
keyVerses.why: The command's decisive measure is Jesus's own self-giving love.

keyVerses.text: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”
keyVerses.why: The visible credibility of discipleship rests on practiced mutual love.

questions.question: What does loving ‘to the end’ mean?
questions.answer: The Greek eis telos can mean to the end, completely, or to the uttermost. John lets both senses work: Jesus loves through the final events and shows love's full extent in service and death. The phrase frames everything that follows, so betrayal and crucifixion are not interruptions of love but the setting where it reaches completion.

questions.question: Why is footwashing so startling?
questions.answer: Dusty roads and sandals made washing feet ordinary hospitality, but the task belonged to people of low household status and could carry deep social humiliation. Jesus knowingly rises from the place of host and teacher, dresses like a servant, and performs it himself. The reversal does not deny his lordship; verse 13 insists that this is what his lordship looks like.

questions.question: Why does Peter first refuse and then demand a full bath?
questions.answer: Peter recognizes the status reversal but still resists receiving it. Jesus says that without being washed Peter has no share with him; Peter then overcorrects as if more washing guaranteed more participation. Jesus distinguishes louō, bathing the whole body, from niptō, washing a part such as feet. The exchange concerns receiving Jesus's cleansing before imitating his service.

questions.question: Is footwashing a required ritual or a broader pattern?
questions.answer: Jesus commands disciples to wash one another's feet and says he gave a hypodeigma, an example or pattern. Some Christian communities rightly practice literal footwashing; all are bound by the enacted logic of accepting low-status, embodied service. Turning it into ceremony while preserving hierarchy and avoiding costly care would miss the example.

questions.question: Why is verse 16's ‘sent one’ important?
questions.answer: John uses apostolos, ‘one who is sent,’ only here in the Gospel, though the verb ‘send’ is central throughout. A messenger is not greater than the sender, just as a servant is not greater than the master. Jesus's own sent identity becomes the shape of discipleship: authority is derivative and accountable, never grounds for refusing the Master's humble pattern.

questions.question: Who is the disciple ‘whom Jesus loved’?
questions.answer: The figure reclines close enough to lean back and ask Jesus privately, later appears at the cross and tomb, and is associated with the Gospel's testimony. John never names him in the narrative. Tradition identifies him with John son of Zebedee, but responsible reading preserves the text's anonymity and attends to his literary role as intimate witness.

questions.question: What does ‘and it was night’ communicate?
questions.answer: Night is literal meal-time, but after John's recurring light-darkness contrast it also carries symbolic weight. Judas receives a morsel of hospitality and goes out to betray Jesus. The narrator's four plain words mark the moral darkness of the choice without making Judas a figure for an ethnic group; every person in the room is Jewish.

questions.question: In what sense is the love command ‘new’?
questions.answer: Torah already commands love of neighbor, so novelty is not the discovery of love. The new measure is kathōs—‘just as’ or ‘in the manner that’ Jesus has loved—and that love is now moving toward the cross. The command also forms a new-covenant community whose identity becomes visible through mutual self-giving rather than claimed superiority.

questions.question: Why place Peter's brave promise beside the love command?
questions.answer: Peter sincerely offers his life but does not yet understand either Jesus's path or his own fear. Jesus predicts three denials before the rooster crows. The placement prevents disciples from imagining that hearing the command makes them heroic; the love Jesus requires begins with receiving mercy for failed self-confidence and will later restore Peter to service.

glossary.def: To the end, completely, or to the uttermost; a compact description of Jesus's love.
Greek verbs for washing a body part and bathing the whole person, contrasted in Jesus's reply to Peter.
An example or pattern intended for imitation.
